docs.title: Welcome to LangGraph RAG
docs.text:
This documentation covers the LangGraph RAG Agent project.

LangGraph RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) helps you build an AI agent that can retrieve knowledge from documents, perform reasoning, and provide answers dynamically.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Retrieval-augmented generation
  • Multi-document support
  • Easy integration with LangGraph and OpenAI
  • Fully containerized with Docker
  • CI/CD ready deployment to GitHub Pages

docs.title: 50 Real-Life Scenario Questions for Pattern Identification
Two Pointers
docs.text:
1. You’re standing at opposite ends of a playground with a friend and want to meet in the middle as fast as possible. Which strategy do you use?
  2. Two people are holding ropes from opposite ends and want to find where they cross.
  3. You have a sorted list of books by height and want to find two books that sum up to exactly 20 cm.
  4. Two runners start at opposite ends of a track and try to catch each other.
  5. You are matching pairs of socks from a sorted pile to minimize mismatch.

docs.title: Sliding Window
docs.text:
1. You are monitoring temperature for the last 7 days and want to find the maximum average temperature.
  2. You want to find the longest period where a child’s heartbeat stays within a safe range.
  3. You are tracking steps over a week and want to find the period with maximum activity.
  4. You are watching traffic and want to find the maximum number of cars passing in any 10-minute interval.
  5. You are streaming video and need to find the longest segment without buffering.

docs.title: Fast & Slow Pointers
docs.text:
1. You have a carousel spinning and want to detect if a horse loops back to the same position.
  2. You want to find the middle step in a staircase to install a railing.
  3. You are following a repeated dance pattern and want to detect if it repeats infinitely.
  4. Two trains start at different speeds on the same track and may meet in a loop — how to detect a collision?
  5. You are checking if a car is driving in circles in a parking lot.

docs.title: DFS / Backtracking
docs.text:
1. You are trying all possible routes in a maze to find all exits.
  2. You are arranging seating combinations for a wedding table.
  3. You are trying all PIN combinations for a lock.
  4. You are exploring all possible moves in a chess game.
  5. You are planning all possible itineraries for a holiday trip.
  6. You are filling a Sudoku board recursively.
  7. You want to generate all possible passwords using certain letters.
  8. You are finding all possible unique pizza toppings combinations.
  9. You are arranging books in all possible orders on a shelf.
  10. You are exploring all possible paths to deliver packages in a city.

docs.title: BFS / Queue
docs.text:
1. You are spreading a rumor in a classroom and want to know how many people hear it each minute.
  2. You are rescuing people in a building level by level.
  3. You want to find the shortest path from your home to the supermarket through streets.
  4. You are modeling water spreading from a leak in a house.
  5. You are passing a message through a chain of friends and want to see who hears it first.
  6. You are finding the shortest sequence of moves to solve a puzzle.
  7. You are mapping the quickest route for delivery drones to reach customers.
  8. You are checking infection spread in a hospital floor.
  9. You are simulating email propagation in a company.
  10. You are finding the minimum steps to reach a target in a game.

docs.title: Stack
docs.text:
1. You are stacking boxes and want to remove the top box first.
  2. You are checking if nested boxes are correctly placed inside each other.
  3. You are undoing actions in a text editor.
  4. You are processing tasks in reverse order of arrival.
  5. You are evaluating math expressions written in reverse polish notation.
  6. You are balancing parentheses in a document.
  7. You are navigating a website with “back” functionality.
  8. You are reversing a list of commands.
  9. You are checking the most recent operation in a calculator.
  10. You are managing browser tabs in reverse order of usage.

docs.title: Queue
docs.text:
1. You are lining up people to buy tickets and serve them first-come-first-serve.
  2. You are modeling customer service calls and answering in order of arrival.
  3. You are managing a printer queue for documents.
  4. You are scheduling tasks to run one after another in a workflow.
  5. You are processing messages in a chat app in the order they arrive.

docs.title: How to Use These 50 Scenarios
docs.text:
1. Read the scenario carefully.

  2. Ask yourself:

  3. Is it about contiguous sequence? → Sliding Window

  4. Is it about matching or reversal? → Stack
  5. Is it about first-come-first-serve? → Queue
  6. Is it about exploring paths/possibilities? → DFS / Backtracking
  7. Is it about shortest distance or level-by-level exploration? → BFS
  8. Is it about detecting loops or finding middle? → Fast & Slow Pointers
  9. Is it about finding a pair or comparing two ends? → Two Pointers
  10. Try to explain why you chose a pattern — that builds intuition.

docs.title: LeetCode Patterns - Base Template
docs.text: This is a base template for documenting all 8 common LeetCode patterns. You can fill in examples, Python starter code, scenarios, and notes for each pattern.

docs.title: 1. Two Pointers
docs.text:
Description:

  • Compare or find pairs from two ends of an array or string.

Python Template:

left, right = 0, len(arr) - 1
while left < right:
    # Your logic here
    left += 1
    right -= 1

docs.title: 2. Sliding Window
docs.text:
Description:

  • Maintain a window of size k to track information over contiguous subarrays or substrings.

Python Template:

window_sum = sum(arr[:k])
for i in range(len(arr) - k):
    window_sum = window_sum - arr[i] + arr[i+k]
    # Your logic here

docs.title: 3. Fast & Slow Pointers
docs.text:
Description:

  • Two pointers moving at different speeds to detect cycles or find middle elements.

Python Template:

slow = fast = head
while fast and fast.next:
    slow = slow.next
    fast = fast.next.next
    if slow == fast:
        # Cycle detected

docs.title: 4. DFS / Backtracking
docs.text:
Description:

  • Explore all paths recursively or iteratively, useful for generating combinations/permutations.

Python Template:

def dfs(node, path):
    # Base case
    for neighbor in graph[node]:
        if neighbor not in visited:
            dfs(neighbor, path)

docs.title: 5. BFS / Queue
docs.text:
Description:

  • Explore nodes level by level using a queue.

Python Template:

from collections import deque
queue = deque([start])
while queue:
    node = queue.popleft()
    for neighbor in graph[node]:
        queue.append(neighbor)

docs.title: 6. Stack
docs.text:
Description:

  • LIFO data structure, useful for reversals, parentheses matching, and DFS iterative implementation.

Python Template:

stack = []
stack.append(item)
while stack:
    item = stack.pop()
    # Your logic here

docs.title: 7. Queue
docs.text:
Description:

  • FIFO data structure, useful for BFS, scheduling, or streaming problems.

Python Template:

from collections import deque
queue = deque()
queue.append(item)
while queue:
    item = queue.popleft()
    # Your logic here

docs.title: 8. Binary Search
docs.text:
Description:

  • Efficiently search in sorted arrays or answer space by halving the search range.

Python Template:

left, right = 0, len(arr) - 1
while left <= right:
    mid = (left + right) // 2
    if arr[mid] == target:
        break
    elif arr[mid] < target:
        left = mid + 1
    else:
        right = mid - 1

docs.title: 9. Linked List Pattern
docs.text: Description: Manipulating nodes, reversing, merging, detecting cycles.

docs.title: Reverse Linked List
docs.text:
prev, curr = None, head
while curr:
    nxt = curr.next
    curr.next = prev
    prev = curr
    curr = nxt
return prev

docs.title: 10. Tree Traversal (DFS & BFS)
docs.text:
Binary tree traversals are fundamental patterns for solving tree problems.

DFS (Depth-First Traversals) 1. Inorder Traversal (Left → Root → Right)

def inorder(root):
    if not root: return
    inorder(root.left)
    print(root.val)
    inorder(root.right)
  1. Preorder Traversal (Root → Left → Right)
def preorder(root):
    if not root: return
    print(root.val)
    preorder(root.left)
    preorder(root.right)
  1. Postorder Traversal (Left → Right → Root)
def postorder(root):
    if not root: return
    postorder(root.left)
    postorder(root.right)
    print(root.val)
  1. BFS (Level Order Traversal)
from collections import deque

def bfs(root):
    if not root: return
    queue = deque([root])
    while queue:
        node = queue.popleft()
        print(node.val)
        if node.left:
            queue.append(node.left)
        if node.right:
            queue.append(node.right)

🔑 When to use what?

Inorder → Sorted output for BSTs.

Preorder → Useful for copying tree / serialization.

Postorder → Useful for deleting tree / bottom-up calculations.

BFS → Best for shortest path, level-wise problems.

docs.title: Python Basics
docs.text:
Got it! I’ll rewrite your Python basics scenarios in beginner-friendly question format, explaining when to use range() vs a list directly, and include tips for using loops, conditions, collections, and built-ins. I’ll also remove tables and make it more like a practice Markdown file.

Here’s the improved version:

docs.title: Python Basics - Scenario-Based Practice
docs.text: This document provides 40 beginner-friendly scenarios to practice Python basics, including loops, conditions, collections, and common built-in functions. Each scenario includes an explanation, when to use certain constructs, and a coding example.

docs.title: 1. For Loops
docs.text:
Tip:

  • Use for x in list when you already have a list of items you want to iterate over.

  • Use for i in range(start, stop, step) when you want to iterate over numbers, especially if you need indices or a specific numeric range. Scenarios:

  • Print all student names in a class

students = ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie']
for name in students:
    print(name)

Use this when you have a predefined list of items.

  1. Count how many numbers in a list are even
nums = [2, 5, 6, 7, 8]
count = 0
for n in nums:
    if n % 2 == 0:
        count += 1
print(count)
  1. Print each character of a word
word = "Python"
for c in word:
    print(c)
  1. Sum the first 50 natural numbers
total = 0
for i in range(1, 51):  # Use range when you want numbers from 1 to 50
    total += i
print(total)
  1. Print items with index
tasks = ['Task1', 'Task2', 'Task3']
for i, task in enumerate(tasks, 1):
    print(i, task)

Use enumerate() when you want both the index and value.

docs.title: 2. While Loops
docs.text:
Tip: Use while loops when the number of iterations is unknown or depends on a condition being met.

  1. Ask user for input until they type 'exit'
inp = ''
while inp != 'exit':
    inp = input("Enter something (type 'exit' to quit): ")
  1. Countdown from 10 to 1
n = 10
while n > 0:
    print(n)
    n -= 1
  1. Empty a list
lst = [1,2,3]
while lst:
    lst.pop()
print(lst)
  1. Guessing game
num = 7
guess = 0
while guess != num:
    guess = int(input("Guess the number: "))
print("Correct!")
  1. Charge battery to 100%
battery = 0
while battery < 100:
    battery += 10
print("Battery full!")

docs.title: 3. If / Else / Elif
docs.text:
Tip: Use if/elif/else when you want to branch code based on conditions.

  1. Check number sign
n = -5
if n > 0:
    print('Positive')
elif n < 0:
    print('Negative')
else:
    print('Zero')
  1. Pass/fail student
marks = 65
if marks >= 50:
    print('Pass')
else:
    print('Fail')
  1. Age category
age = 15
if age < 13:
    print('Child')
elif age < 20:
    print('Teen')
else:
    print('Adult')
  1. Discount based on purchase
price = 70
if price > 100:
    discount = 10
elif price > 50:
    discount = 5
else:
    discount = 0
print(discount)
  1. Check palindrome
word = 'radar'
if word == word[::-1]:
    print('Yes')
else:
    print('No')

docs.title: 4. Lists
docs.text:
Tip: Use lists when you want an ordered, changeable collection.

  1. Store daily temperatures
temps = [23, 25, 22]
  1. Shopping list add/remove
items = ['Eggs', 'Bread']
items.append('Milk')
items.remove('Eggs')
  1. Reverse names
names = ['Alice', 'Bob']
print(names[::-1])
  1. Merge two student lists
list1 = ['Alice', 'Bob']
list2 = ['Charlie']
all_students = list1 + list2
  1. Max/min scores
scores = [55, 89, 76]
print(max(scores))
print(min(scores))

docs.title: 5. Tuples
docs.text:
Tip: Use tuples for fixed, unchangeable data.

  1. Store coordinates
coord = (10, 20)
  1. Month and days
month = ('Jan', 31)
  1. Student info fixed
student = (1, 'Alice')
  1. RGB colors
color = (255, 0, 0)
  1. Configuration settings
settings = ('High', 'ON')

docs.title: 6. Sets
docs.text:
Tip: Use sets for unique items or membership checks.

  1. Remove duplicate names
names = ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Alice']
unique_names = set(names)
  1. Track unique words
text = "hello world hello"
words = set(text.split())
  1. Check prime membership
primes = {2, 3, 5, 7}
n = 3
if n in primes:
    print("Prime")
  1. Common friends
friends1 = {'Alice', 'Bob'}
friends2 = {'Bob', 'Charlie'}
common = friends1 & friends2
  1. Unique user IDs
ids = [1, 2, 2, 3]
user_ids = set(ids)

docs.title: 7. Dictionaries
docs.text:
Tip: Use dicts for key-value storage.

  1. Store marks by name
marks = {'Alice': 90, 'Bob': 85}
  1. Word frequency
words = ['hello', 'world', 'hello']
freq = {}
for w in words:
    freq[w] = freq.get(w, 0) + 1
print(freq)
  1. Product prices
prices = {'Milk': 50}
  1. Employee roles
roles = {'John': 'Manager'}
  1. Country codes
codes = {'US': 1, 'IN': 91}

docs.title: 8. Enumerate
docs.text:
Tip: Use enumerate() to get index and value together.

tasks = ['Task1', 'Task2']
for i, t in enumerate(tasks, 1):
    print(i, t)

docs.title: 9. Zip
docs.text:
Tip: Use zip() to combine lists element-wise.

names = ['Alice', 'Bob']
marks = [90, 85]
for n, m in zip(names, marks):
    print(n, m)

docs.title: 10. itertools
docs.text:
Tip: Use itertools for combinatorial tasks like permutations and combinations.

from itertools import permutations, combinations

people = ['A', 'B']
for p in permutations(people):
    print(p)

menu = ['Pizza', 'Burger']
for c in combinations(menu, 2):
    print(c)

docs.title: 11. functools
docs.text:
Tip: Use functools.reduce() to aggregate a list into a single value.

from functools import reduce
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]
product = reduce(lambda x, y: x * y, nums)
print(product)

Usage Tips for Beginners:

  • Use range() in for loops when you need numeric sequences or indices.
  • Use for x in list when you have predefined elements to iterate.
  • Use while loops when the end condition is unknown.
  • Use enumerate() when you need index + value.
  • Use zip() to combine two lists element-wise.
  • Use set for unique items, tuple for immutable collections, and dict for key-value pairs.
  • itertools and functools help with advanced iterations and reductions.

Here’s a quick list you could add to your Markdown under “Built-in Functions” for beginners:

docs.title: 12. Useful Built-in Functions
docs.text:
Tip: Python has many built-in functions to make common tasks easy.

  1. Sum of numbers in a list
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
total = sum(nums)
print(total)
  1. Maximum and minimum
scores = [55, 89, 76]
print(max(scores))  # 89
print(min(scores))  # 55
  1. Length of a list/string
names = ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie']
print(len(names))  # 3

word = "Python"
print(len(word))   # 6
  1. Sorted list
nums = [5, 2, 9, 1]
print(sorted(nums))  # [1, 2, 5, 9]
  1. Reverse a list
nums = [1, 2, 3]
print(list(reversed(nums)))  # [3, 2, 1]
  1. Absolute value
n = -10
print(abs(n))  # 10
  1. Check if any or all elements are True
lst = [True, False, True]
print(any(lst))  # True
print(all(lst))  # False

💡 Tip for beginners:

  • Use sum() instead of manually looping and adding numbers.
  • max() and min() work for numbers and strings (lexicographical).
  • len() is the easiest way to get size of a list, tuple, string, or dict.
  • sorted() and reversed() give sorted or reversed copies; they do not change the original list unless you use list.sort() or list.reverse().

docs.title: MultiGent: RAG Multi-Agent Pipeline
docs.text: This page describes the RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) Multi-Agent system built using LangGraph and LangChain.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The MultiGent system orchestrates multiple agents to answer questions using external knowledge. It consists of three main agents:

  1. Retriever Agent – fetches relevant documents from a vector store.
  2. Summarizer Agent – summarizes the retrieved documents.
  3. QA Agent – generates answers based on the summarized context.

docs.title: Python Interview Questions and Answers (Beginner → Advanced)
Beginner (Basics, Data Types, Loops, Functions)
docs.text:
1. What is Python? Python is a high-level(human readability,memory management autometically), interpreted language(line by line) known for its simplicity and readability. It supports multiple paradigms like procedural, object-oriented, and functional programming.

  2. What are Python’s key features? Python is interpreted, dynamically typed, and object-oriented. It has a rich standard library and allows easy integration with other languages and tools.

  3. What is PEP 8? PEP 8 is Python’s style guide that defines conventions for writing readable and consistent code. Following it improves maintainability and collaboration.

  4. Difference between Python 2 and Python 3? Python 3 uses print() as a function, supports Unicode by default, and division returns a float. Python 2 uses print as a statement and integer division truncates results.

    Feature Python 2 Python 3 String type str = bytes (ASCII only) str = Unicode by default Unicode string u"hello" "hello" (always Unicode) Byte string "hello" (by default) b"hello" Emoji support Hard to handle Works out-of-the-box Operation Python 2 Output Python 3 Output 5 / 2 2 (int) 2.5 (float) 5 / 2.0 2.5 (float) 2.5 (float) 5 // 2 2 (floor) 2 (floor) Expression Python 2 Result Python 3 Result 7 / 3 2 (truncated) 2.333... (float) 7 / 4 1 (truncated) 1.75 (float) 7 // 3 2 2 7 // 4 1 1

  5. What are Python’s data types? Python has types like int, float, str, list, tuple, set, dict, bool, and NoneType. Each type helps store and manipulate specific kinds of data.

  6. Mutable vs Immutable types? Mutable types (list, dict, set) can be changed after creation. Immutable types (tuple, str, int, float) cannot, affecting how they behave in memory.

  7. What is Python’s indentation rule? Python uses indentation to define code blocks instead of braces {}. Proper indentation is mandatory to avoid syntax errors.

  8. What are comments in Python? Single-line comments use #. Multi-line comments use triple quotes ''' or """. They are ignored during execution.

  9. What are Python’s built-in functions for collections? Common ones include len(), sum(), max(), min(), sorted(), and reversed(). These simplify operations on lists, sets, tuples, and dictionaries.

  10. Difference between list and tuple? Lists are mutable and slower, while tuples are immutable, faster, and use less memory. Use tuples for fixed data and lists for changeable data.

  11. Difference between list and set? Lists are ordered and allow duplicates, sets are unordered and store only unique elements. Sets are efficient for membership tests.

  12. Difference between == and is? == checks value equality, while is checks object identity in memory. Use is to compare object references.

  13. How to remove duplicates from a list? Convert to a set and back: unique = list(set(lst)). This removes duplicates but may reorder elements.

  14. How to iterate over a list? Use for item in list for values, or for i in range(len(list)) for indices. enumerate() is preferred for index + value.

  15. What is a function in Python? A function is a reusable block of code that performs a task. It can accept parameters and return values using return.

docs.title: Intermediate (OOP, Modules, File Handling, Error Handling)
docs.text:
1. What is *args and **kwargs? *args passes a variable number of positional arguments, while **kwargs passes variable keyword arguments. They make functions flexible.

  2. What is a lambda function? Lambda is an anonymous, single-line function used for simple operations. Example: square = lambda x: x**2.

  3. Difference between @staticmethod and @classmethod? @staticmethod does not access class or instance data, while @classmethod takes the class itself as the first parameter. Both decorate methods differently.

    Feature @staticmethod @classmethod First argument None cls (the class itself) Access instance data ❌ No ❌ No Access class data ❌ No ✅ Yes Usage Utility/helper functions Work with class-level data/constructors Feature Inheritance Polymorphism Encapsulation Definition Derive properties & methods from another class Same method call behaves differently for different objects Hides internal details of an object Purpose Code reuse, hierarchy Flexibility, dynamic behavior Data protection, controlled access Example class Dog(Animal) dog.speak(), cat.speak() Private variables __balance Key Concept "is-a" relationship Method overriding / operator overloading Data hiding / getter & setter

  4. What is inheritance? Inheritance allows a class to derive properties and methods from another class. It promotes code reuse and hierarchy.

  5. What is polymorphism? Polymorphism allows different objects to respond to the same method call in different ways. It includes method overriding and operator overloading.

  6. What is encapsulation? Encapsulation hides internal object details using private variables. Access is provided via getter/setter methods.

    Access Type Prefix Accessible From Notes Public None Anywhere No restriction Protected/Semi-Private _ Class & Subclasses Discouraged from outside Private __ Class only (name-mangled) Full encapsulation

  7. Difference between class variable and instance variable? Class variables are shared across instances; instance variables are unique per object. Both are used for storing data in classes.

  8. What is super()? super() allows calling parent class methods from a child class. It is commonly used in constructors to initialize inherited attributes.

  9. What are decorators? Decorators modify the behavior of a function or class without changing its code. They are commonly used for logging, validation, or access control.

  10. How to read and write files? Use with open('file.txt', 'r') as f: to read and with open('file.txt', 'w') as f: to write. with ensures files are properly closed.

  11. Difference between read(), readline(), readlines()? read() reads the entire file, readline() reads one line, readlines() returns a list of lines. Use based on memory and processing needs.

    Method What it does Use Case read() Reads the entire file as a string Small files where you need all content readline() Reads one line at a time Large files, line-by-line processing readlines() Reads all lines into a list Need to iterate over lines multiple times

  12. Difference between import module and from module import function? import module requires prefixing with module.func(), from module import func allows direct access to func().

  13. What is __name__ == "__main__"? It checks whether the script is executed directly or imported as a module. Code under this runs only when the file is executed directly.

  14. How to handle exceptions? Use try-except blocks to catch errors. Example:

try: x=1/0
except ZeroDivisionError: print("Cannot divide by zero")
  1. Difference between finally and else in try-except? finally executes always, regardless of errors. else executes only if no exception occurs.

docs.title: Advanced (Advanced OOP, Iterators, Generators, Concurrency, Modules)
docs.text:
1. What is Python GIL? The Global Interpreter Lock allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time. It limits CPU-bound multi-threading.

  2. Difference between multithreading and multiprocessing? Threading runs multiple threads in shared memory, limited by GIL. Multiprocessing uses separate processes for true parallelism.

  3. What is a generator? A generator is an iterator that yields values one at a time using yield. It is memory-efficient for large datasets.

  4. Difference between yield and return? return sends a value and exits the function. yield sends a value but pauses function execution, resuming later.

  5. What are iterators? Iterators implement __iter__() and __next__() methods to traverse collections. Generators are a special kind of iterator.

  6. Difference between deep copy and shallow copy? Shallow copy copies the object structure but references nested objects. Deep copy duplicates the object and all nested elements independently.

  7. What is a context manager (with statement)? with ensures resources are properly managed (like files). It automatically closes files or releases resources after use.

  8. What are comprehensions? Python comprehensions provide concise syntax to create lists, sets, and dictionaries. Example: [x**2 for x in range(5)].

  9. Difference between is and ==? is checks if two objects are identical in memory, == checks if values are equal. Use is for object identity.

  10. Difference between del and remove()? del lst[0] deletes by index, lst.remove(val) deletes by value. del can also remove variables entirely.

  11. What is a Python module? A module is a file containing Python code (functions, classes, variables) that can be reused in other programs. Modules improve code organization.

  12. What is a package? A package is a collection of modules organized in directories with __init__.py. Packages allow modular project structures.

  13. Popular Python libraries for data? numpy, pandas, matplotlib, seaborn, scikit-learn, requests, json. They cover computation, visualization, and web access.

  14. Difference between Python array and list? Lists can hold mixed data types; arrays (from array module or numpy) hold elements of the same type and are more memory efficient.

  15. How to manage dependencies in Python? Use pip for installing packages, and requirements.txt to track dependencies. Virtual environments isolate project packages.

  16. What is Python’s itertools module? itertools provides efficient iterators for combinations, permutations, and Cartesian products. Useful for algorithmic tasks.

  17. What is Python’s functools module? functools provides higher-order functions like reduce(), partial(), and decorators. It simplifies functional programming tasks.

  18. How to profile Python code? Use the cProfile module to measure execution time and function calls. Profiling identifies performance bottlenecks.

  19. What is monkey patching? Monkey patching modifies or extends modules/classes at runtime. It can fix bugs or add features without modifying original code.

  20. Difference between Python threads and asyncio? Threads run concurrently with shared memory but limited by GIL. asyncio uses cooperative multitasking with async/await for I/O-bound tasks.

This categorization makes it easier to target questions based on skill level:

  • Beginner: Basics, data types, loops, functions
  • Intermediate: OOP, file handling, error handling, modules
  • Advanced: Iterators, generators, concurrency, performance, advanced OOP
